messages.subject_clean: R CFA lavaan and Common Method Bias (syntax)
messages.body_plain:
Here is an example:

library(lavaan); library(MASS); set.seed(22)

Lambda <- cbind(rep(1,12), diag(3)[rep(1:3,each=4),])

rownames(Lambda) <- paste("x",1:12,sep="")

Sigma <- Lambda %*% t(Lambda) + diag(12)

data <- mvrnorm(100,rep(0,12),Sigma)

#cfa("M1 =~ x1 + x2 + x3 + x4

#     M2 =~ x5 + x6 + x7 + x8

#     G =~ x1 + x2 + x3 + x4 + x5 + x6 + x7 + x8", data)

cfa("M1 =~ x1 + x2 + x3 + x4

     M2 =~ x5 + x6 + x7 + x8

     M3 =~ x9 + x10 + x11 + x12

     G =~ x1 + x2 + x3 + x4 + x5 + x6 + x7 + x8 + x9 + x10 + x11 + x12", data)

The example also shows why we should not trust these models: they are often empirically underidentified. The example comes from my lecture on identification of these models. You can find the code in the notes of slide 25.

Best regards,

Mikko

messages.subject: Understanding aberrant fit index values
messages.subject_clean: Understanding aberrant fit index values
messages.body_plain:
I'm using lavaan for the first time and have come across what looks like an aberrant fit index value in the summary obtained after fitting a CFA model. I'd like to better understand whether/why this is the case.

Some context: The data are not mine, but taken from OSF, and contain almost 40000 responses to 16 items intending to measure the "dark factor" of personality. I'm trying to run a CFA in which responses to all 16 items load on a single D-factor. Each response is given on a 5-point ordinal scale.

I've specified the model thus:
cfaFormula1 <- 'D =~ d1 + d2 + d3 + d4 + d5 + d6 + d7 + d8 +
d9 + d10 + d11 + d12 + d13 + d14 + d15 + d16'

And then am fitting it using the following command:
cfa1 <- cfa(cfaFormula1,
            data = mp,
            ordered = TRUE,
            estimator = "PML")

(Note that I specified the estimator as PML because I want to be able to compare models using BIC, and as far as I'm aware that is the only option for doing this with ordinal variables in lavaan---though as I say, I'm new to the package so please correct me if this is wrong.)

I then obtain a summary of the outcome thus:
summary(cfa1, standardized = TRUE, fit.measures = TRUE)

This gives me the following output (trimmed):
lavaan 0.6-19 ended normally after 67 iterations

  Estimator                                        PML
  Optimization method                           NLMINB
  Number of model parameters                        80

  Number of observations                         37744

Model Test User Model:
                                              Standard      Scaled
  Test Statistic                              8808.631   14493.473
  Degrees of freedom                               104     115.277
  P-value (Unknown)                                 NA       0.000
  Scaling correction factor                                  0.608
    mean+var adjusted correction (PML)

Model Test Baseline Model:

  Test statistic                            537882.605   48902.728
  Degrees of freedom                               120      12.177
  P-value                                           NA       0.000
  Scaling correction factor                                 10.999

User Model versus Baseline Model:

  Comparative Fit Index (CFI)                    0.984       0.706
  Tucker-Lewis Index (TLI)                       0.981       0.969

My confusion here lies in the CFI and TLI values listed in the "Scaled" column. As I understand it (from here <https://davidakenny.net/cm/fit.htm>), the CFI is calculated as (d(baseline) - d(user))/d(baseline), where d(x) = \chi^2(x) - df(x). From the scaled values provided in the output, I can manually calculate the scaled CFI as:

 ((48902 - 12) - (14493 - 115)) / (48902 - 12)
 ~ = .701
Given my rounding, this is basically consistent with the reported output.

If the TLI is calculated as (\chi^2(baseline)/df(baseline) - \chi^2(user)/df(user)) / (\chi^2(baseline)/df(baseline) - 1), then I get:

 (48902/12 - 14493/115) / (48902/12 - 1)
~ = .969
Given my rounding, this is again consistent with the reported output. So, both of the indices seem to be calculated correctly. Where I am confused is simply that the CFI is so much lower than the TLI, whereas everything I've read seems to suggest that the opposite should be true. The page I linked above does mention that the CFI will be too low if the RMSEA of the baseline model is less than .158, but when I run nullRMSEA(cfa1, scaled = TRUE) I get a value substantially higher than that (.345).

Can anyone help me shed some light on this, so I can better understand what's going on and why?

Thanks in advance.

messages.body_plain:
Dear all,

The next 'Psychoco' (=psychometric computing) workshop will be held at
the University of Ghent (Belgium), 6 + 7 Feb 2025.

The aim of this workshop is to bring together researchers from
statistics, psychology, and related disciplines working on modern
techniques for the analysis of data from psychology and the social
sciences. Following the fruitful previous workshops, it will provide a
platform for discussions about implementation and application of
software on the interface of statistical inference, computational
methods, and applied psychometrics. A special emphasis is given to
implementations in the R system for statistical computing. To create a
diverse and inspiring program, both authors and users of psychometric
software packages are encouraged to present their recent and ongoing work.

Submission deadline: 	December 15, 2024
Registration deadline: 	January 12, 2025

Workshop participation is free of charge, but you must register. For
more information, go to the website:

https://www.psychoco.org/2025/index.html

Yves.

--
Yves Rosseel
Department of Data Analysis, Ghent University

https://lavaan.org/about/donate.html

Yuval,

There are many experts on the list who have experience in doing and writing about RI/CLPM (including myself.) What you are basically asking is if anyone is willing to do consulting for you. This depends on your willingness to pay. When you make this kind of request, it would be useful to give some indication of how large budget you have.

For example, my consulting rate is 400$/h. Why such high rate? Because I (and many others)prefer to help people publicly or spend our private time on our own projects. However, if someone values my advice sufficiently to pay the consulting rate, I would be interested in at least hearing what the problem that they have is.

You can find statistical consultants for example here:

https://instats.org/?v=experts

https://www.goquantfish.com

https://statisticalhorizons.com/consulting/

On the other hand, if you just post your question here, you will likely get a response for free. This is because by answering your question on the list, experts contribute to the community and because the answer to your question may also be helpful for someone else.

Best regards,

Mikko

messages.body_plain:
Hi, Peter,

TLI and CFI tend to have a very high correlation, but both can vary a lot depending on sample size, number and type of items, model type and so on. In a paper I am writing, my colleagues and I simulated more than 1.2 million datasets and the mean correlation between CFI and TLI was 0.851, but there were some some cases when the correlation was as low as 0.3.
I'm unaware about studies that focused on this specific correlation though.

Best,
Yago

messages.body_plain:
Hi, Peter.

Since this isn't our main question, I never thought much about that. While I was summarizing the data for the first time, I had the impression that the main source of discordance occurs when you fit more latent variables than exist in the population model. This leads to overfitting, with the CFI having an upper limit of 1, while TLI has no upper limit.

I tried to fit a lm, but due to the sample size, everything is statistically significant. Based on the effect sizes, I would say that the variables that really affect the correlation between CFI and TLI are:
 - Estimator (partial Eta²: 0.30 [0.26-0.33]): Compared to MLR, WLSMV lowers the correlation when `ordered = FALSE` (B: -0.185, SE: 0.017, t: -10.763, p < 2e-16), but not when `ordered = TRUE` (B: -0.024, SE: 0.018, t: -1.363, p = 0.173).
 - Fittel model (partial Eta²: 0.19 [0.15-0.22]): Compared to fitting a bifactor model, the correlation increases when fitting a unidimensional model (B: 0.216, SE: 0.019, t: 11.373, p < 2e-16) or a first-order bidimensional model (B: 0.195, SE: 0.019, t: 10.254, p  < 2e-16).
 - Population model (partial Eta²: 0.11 [0.08-0.14]): Compared to having a bifactor structure in the population, the correlation decreases when the structure is unidimensional model (B: -0.069, SE: 0.020, t: -3.444, p = 5.91e-4) or a first-order bidimensional structure (B: -0.049, SE: 0.020, t: -2.458, p  0.014).

Please, note that the aim of the study was not to explore the correlation between CFI and TLI, which is not even published yet, and these results are a shallow exploration I did after your question. So, I am not sure how generalizable they are.

Obs.: MLR cannot be used when `ordered = TRUE`. Thus, the estimator has three levels: MLR with `ordered = FALSE` (includes analysis with truly continuous items and with ordinal items treated as continuous), WLSMV with `ordered = FALSE` (same as before), and WLSMV with `ordered = TRUE` (only ordinal items)

Best,
Yago

Dear lavaan contributors,

I’m currently working on fitting a simple CFA model (4 observed variables, 1 latent variable) using the correlation matrix of the observed variables.

In reviewing literature (e.g., Cudeck, 1989), I’ve come across discussions about the potential issues with fitting non-scale-invariant models on correlation matrices.

I’m wondering if anyone could offer insights or recommend resources to clarify whether using a correlation matrix in the cfa() function in lavaan might affect the accuracy of the omnibus test statistic or standard errors.

Here is the code I’m using:

model <- 'LV1 =~ MV1 + MV2 + MV3 + MV4'
fit <- lavaan::cfa(model, sample.cov=COR.matrix, std.lv <http://std.lv>=T, sample.nobs = 250)

Thank you very much for your help.

Kind regards,

Laura
REF: Cudeck, R. (1989). Analysis of correlation matrices using covariance structure models. Psychological bulletin, 105(2), 317.

            LatentFactor1 =~ Var1 + Var3 + Var4

Hello Laura,

Recent versions of lavaan now have a correlation = TRUE option, which
allows for the analysis of correlation matrices. Only the GLS and WLS
estimators are supported. (I don't think it is possible using ML, but I
may be wrong).

What happens behind the scenes:

1) the 'residual' variances of the indicators are no longer 'free'
parameters; their values are set so that the total variance is one

2) the 'Gamma' matrix (normal-based, or ADF) is modified to reflect the
sampling variability of the elements in a correlation matrix (excluding
the unit diagonal)

This should lead to correct standard errors for the model parameters,
and 'robust' fit measures.

I should perhaps add that this 'feature' is relatively new/experimental,
and more simulation studies are needed to verify that it works correctly.

As for literature: there is not much. But there is this book chapter:

Bentler, P. and Savalei, V. (2010). Analysis of correlation structures:
current status and open problems. In "Statistics in the Social
Sciences', edited by Kolenikov S., Steinley, D, Thombs, L.

(I can send you a pdf offline; just email me).

Yves.

May I ask one quick question? Is the following correlation matrix among latent variables the one with the warning?

>
> 1.000
> 0.882 1.000
> 0.675 0.868 1.000
> 0.850 0.913 0.731 1.000
> 0.882 0.902 0.617 0.682 1.000
>

I previously thought that it was the one with a correlation of .975. But I checked and it is the second correlation matrix that is not positive definite. However, I may be wrong due to rounding errors.

I think the problem is more a theoretical one than an SEM one. Even if you got no warning, it is not easy to adopt a model with factor correlations so high (.8 to .9). Is this the measurement model step and do you plan to test a structural model? If this is the case, then the high correlations "may" be meaningful because they reflect strong effects from some factors to other factors. But they may also suggest multicollinearity among the factors.

Putting aside the issue of high correlations, if you just want to remove the warning legitimately, one possible solution came to my mind. Given that the warning is not for the large sample, if theoretically justifiable, you can try constraining the factor variances and covariances to be equal between the two groups (after you have constrained other parameters, such as factor loadings). If this model is so-called true, then the factor variances and covariances estimate the common factor variances and covariances, using data from both samples. (Yes, this is unlikely to be absolutely true ... but many models are approximations and not absolutely true.)

Certainly, this requires that it is theoretically meaningful to impose the constraints. Moreover, there is no guarantee that this can solve the problem, given the large factor correlations in both samples.

-- Shu Fai

Anna--
     You have done a lot of the things that I would have recommended.
     You are estimating a model for ordinal observed variables, so the free parameters include things like threshold values for different levels of the various observed variables. I only get about 55 free parameters for a model with continuous variables and a mean structure. That means 109 additional free parameters to model the ordinality. That suggests that your observed variables have many distinct values, which calls for estimating many thresholds. Do your observed variables have many levels each?
     Here is where your sample size may not be as large as it seems. With 15 substantially correlated observed variables and many levels of each observed variable, you might have a rather thin spread of data points across the cells of several of the bivariate crosstabs for pairs of observed variables. That, in turn, might be creating an estimation problem. It might be worthwhile to examine crosstabs of your observed variables, to see if there are a number of empty or near-empty cells.
     First, though, you migth run your model without the "ordinal" declaration and see if the identification warning is still present.
--Ed Rigdon

I rarely read papers that applied SEM explained why non-positive definite covariance matrix happened.

As explained by others, this may be merely due to sampling error. In my demonstration of the group order, the model fitted is a true model because I know the data generation model. However, due to the small sample size in one group, I could artificially find a possible sample that yields a non-positive definite covariance matrix for the latent variables, as in your case.

Though not ideal, you probably can suggest that that warning may be due to the small sample size in one group. Therefore, when the full sample is used to estimate the parameters, the warning disappears.

However, note that, as far as I know, it is not common to constrain the factor variances and covariances to be equal between groups  (though this can be a desirable model in some cases) because this is a very strict form of equivalence (and so may usually fail to fit well). You may need to see whether you can justify these constraints theoretically.

Hope this helps.

-- Shu Fai

messages.body_plain:
Dear community,

I posted a question on CrossValidated <https://stats.stackexchange.com/questions/657492/best-way-to-report-indirect-effects-in-a-complex-structural-equation-model-sem> a few days ago (which may not have been the best place to start). So I am reproducing my question below.

I am fitting a complex structural equation model (SEM) with 4 latent and 2 observed variables (15 direct and 36 indirect effects). Importantly, in this model, some indirect effects from a given predictor to a given outcome are positive and some are negative (e.g., total effect = 5, but indirect effect 1 = 50, indirect effect 2 = -40, and indirect effect 3 = -5).

To make my analysis easier to understand, I thought about plotting the indirect effects of interest so that the reader could see the main conclusions at a glance.

I have considered several ways of doing this, all of which have advantages and disadvantages, and I cannot decide which is the most appropriate:
Plot the raw indirect effects with the total effect. Pros: It reports all raw results. Cons: In the case of suppression effects, it may be difficult to understand how much the most important indirect pathways contribute to the total effect.
Plot the percentage of a given effect in the total effect. Advantages: Allows the reader to understand the contribution of each indirect effect to the total effect. Disadvantages: Some percentages may be greater than 100 due to suppression effects. This was already mentioned here <https://groups.google.com/g/lavaan/c/_ezFUBC3FJ4/m/4o7aBTHRAgAJ>.
Solution two, but using the absolute total effect. In this solution, I would calculate the absolute total effect by summing the absolute value of the direct and indirect effects. Advantages: I can show the contribution of each mediation to the absolute total effect, with the direction of that mediation. Disadvantages: I sense disadvantages, but I cannot put my finger on them. Hence the question.

Each solution answers a different question, with advantages and disadvantages. I have come to mixed conclusions on my own, and definitely need an outside view on what you think is the most important information to convey to the reader in the main text (other interesting solutions may still find their way into the appendix).

> Plot the raw indirect effects with the total effect. Pros: It reports all raw results. Cons: In the case of suppression effects, it may be difficult to understand how much the most important indirect pathways contribute to the total effect.
> Plot the percentage of a given effect in the total effect. Advantages: Allows the reader to understand the contribution of each indirect effect to the total effect. Hi all,

I'm just starting with lavaan, so I apologize if this is a really basic question. I'm running the following multilevel mediation model:

mediation_syntax <- '

level: 1
# random intercept for outcome (y; level 1)
y ~ 1

level: 2
# predictor (x; level 2) and covariate (cov; level 2) predict mediators (m1, m2; both at level 2)
m1 ~ a1 * x + d_m1 * cov
m2 ~ a2 * x + d_m2 * cov

# predictor (x), covariate (cov), and mediators (m1, m2) predicts outcome (y)
y ~ b1 * m1 + b2 * m2 + c * x + d_y * cov

# allow mediators to covary
m1 ~~ m2

# define indirect effects
ind1 := a1 * b1
ind2 := a2 * b2

# define total effect
tot := c + ind1 + ind2
'

fit <- lavaan::sem(mediation_syntax, data = dat, cluster = 'level2_id', estimator = 'MLR', fixed.x = FALSE)
param <- lavaan::parameterEstimates(fit)

When I inspect param, I see that the estimate and standard error for `y ~ 1` is zero (row 1 in the below screenshot). Is this an expected behavior or not?

I already double-checked to ensure that `y` is a level 1 variable (i.e., there is some variation in y within a cluster). I also tried running this random intercept-only model:

fit2 <- lavaan::sem("y ~ 1", data = dat, cluster = "level2_id", estimator = 'MLR', fixed.x = FALSE)
param2 <- lavaan::parameterEstimates(fit2)

and it did successfully return an estimate and standard error of `y ~ 1`, so I suspect that something is wrong with the way I set up my mediation model, but can't figure out why.

Any help would be really appreciated. Thank you!

If you are asking, "What will the journals accept?" I have no guidance for you.

I am not the best expert on the ESEM application within lavaan. Generically, you would do things like imposing equity constraints on different parameters (either loadings or residual variances). If the variance of the observed variables are similar, thenequal residual variance might not do too much violence to the data. You could accomplish this by adding syntax like this:

v1~~a*v1
v2~~a*v3
v3~~a*v3
v4~~a*v4
v5~~a*v5

This turns 5 parameters to estimate into 1, but it does impose meaningful constraints, changing the model.

Alternatively, if you had some more specific ideas about which observed variables are responsive to the third common factor, you might represent that joint dependency by allowing some residual covariance within a model with only two common factors.

Hey everyone,

I would like to conduct a mediation analysis in lavaan. I would like to test the effect of age (in years) on a cognitive function, statistical learning (SL). I would like to test if 1) age predicts performance in SL, and 2) if so, this relationship is mediated by age effects in other cognitive factors (perceptual speed [PS], and working memory [WM]).

My mediation model would look like:
-- predictor variable: age
-- outcome variable: SL
-- mediator variables: PS and WM (I would like to include them both in a single model because if mediation occurs, I am curious if they mediate the same shared variability between age and SL)

However, my problem is that age effects in the case of all cognitive abilities (SL, PS and WM) are nonlinear (I think that a quadratic logarithmic function describes them best):

The relationship between the cognitive abilities are linear:

So the relationships (and regressions) within my model would look like:
-- c path: SL ~ age + age^2 (quadratic)
-- a paths: WM ~ age + age^2 and PS ~ age + age^2 (quadratic)

Since no one has responded to my question so far, I believe I may not have been specific enough to provide a clear understanding of the problem. I am available to provide further clarification if needed.

The data used in my analysis comes from the 2010 demographic census conducted by IBGE, the Brazilian agency responsible for that year’s census survey. The data of interest is associated with a specific municipality in the state of Minas Gerais (Brazil), and my research aims to explore causal relationships within families whose per capita household income is up to half the minimum wage.

To create a dataset suitable for use with the lavaan package, the data was sourced from two files. The first file contains census information about households, and the second includes data about individuals surveyed. The CSV file I shared is the result of a probabilistic match, where each individual was randomly assigned to a household within the same income category. The resulting data was then adjusted to a normal distribution and scaled to have a mean of zero and a variance of one.

Thus, the CSV file contains both continuous, binary and categorical data. The categorical variables were adjusted following the approach detailed by Bollen (2014) in Chapter 9 (reference in the end of this message).
